clue.text: God knows man's was over twenty-one

definitions.text: God knows man's was over twenty-one

parts.words: God knows man's was over twenty-one
parts.note: one more than twenty-one is twenty-two, the number in the title of Joseph Heller's war novel, whose airman Yossarian is caught in an absurd rule

explanation.surface: A remark that heaven knows some fellow was past the age of majority.
explanation.walkthrough: Twenty-one is the old age of coming of age, so the surface is about someone's age; really 'over twenty-one' means the next number, 22, as in Heller's title.
explanation.definitionFit: Heller's novel names a self-defeating rule after the number one past twenty-one, so the cryptic description points to its first word.

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'A big noise at (9)' is cut short after 'at'; the rest of the clue (the setting of the noise) is missing from the OCR text.

clue.text: A critic is a man who knows the way but can't drive the car ()

definitions.text: A critic is a man who knows the way but can't drive the car

parts.words: A critic is a man who knows the way but can't drive the car
parts.note: a famous quip about critics, made by the English theatre reviewer Kenneth of the Observer; the clue asks who said it

explanation.surface: A witty saying that critics give directions but cannot do the driving themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is a quotation; the answer is the surname of the theatre critic who coined it.
explanation.definitionFit: The quip is attributed to the celebrated English drama reviewer, so the quotation identifies its speaker.

clue.text: Architect of The Windhover's hunting ground?

parts.note: The Windhover is Gerard Manley Hopkins's poem about a kestrel, a small hawk, so its 's gives the possessive of a hawk
a moor is open upland where grouse and deer are hunted

explanation.surface: Asks who designed the territory over which Hopkins's falcon hunts.
explanation.walkthrough: Hopkins's windhover is a kestrel; the hawk's hunting ground gives the name of Nicholas Hawksmoor, the English Baroque architect of London churches.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicholas Hawksmoor was an English Baroque architect who worked with Wren and designed several London churches.

clue.text: He admiringly recalled a bargewoman

parts.note: in Antony and Cleopatra, Antony's friend gives the famous speech 'The barge she sat in, like a burnish'd throne', praising Cleopatra on the river Cydnus

explanation.surface: Someone fondly remembers a woman who worked on a canal boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bargewoman' suggests a working boatwoman; it is Cleopatra on her barge, described by Antony's officer in Shakespeare's play.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare gives the speech praising Cleopatra on her gilded vessel to Antony's soldier friend, who recalls her with admiration.

clue.text: Poet's measure correct

parts.note: an en is a printer's measure of width, half an em
right means correct, as in 'that's right'

explanation.surface: A verse writer's metre is judged to be accurate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Measure' looks like poetic metre, but it is the printer's unit EN. The 's after 'Poet' stands for 'is', linking the definition to the wordplay; D. J. Enright was an English poet.
explanation.definitionFit: D. J. Enright was an English poet and critic of the Movement generation.

clue.text: Her brother was warned about lending

definitions.text: Her brother was warned about lending

parts.words: Her brother was warned about lending
parts.note: in Hamlet, Polonius tells his son Laertes 'Neither a borrower nor a lender be'; the clue asks for Laertes's sister

explanation.surface: A woman whose sibling was cautioned not to lend money.
explanation.walkthrough: Polonius's advice to Laertes includes 'Neither a borrower nor a lender be'; Laertes's sister is Hamlet's beloved.
explanation.definitionFit: In Hamlet, Polonius's daughter is the sister of Laertes, the son he lectures about lending.

clue.text: A race is suggested by a shepherd of Herodotus

parts.note: TT is the Tourist Trophy, the Isle of Man motorcycle race

explanation.surface: Some contest is hinted at by a herdsman in the Greek historian's work.
explanation.walkthrough: TT is the Tourist Trophy, the famous Isle of Man motorbike race; 'suggested by' is a link. Attis is the Phrygian shepherd loved by Cybele, and Herodotus tells of an Atys.
explanation.definitionFit: Attis is the Phrygian shepherd youth of Greek myth, loved by the goddess Cybele.

clue.text: New Blair mien of Scott's arbiter

indicators.note: new tells us the letters are made into a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: A fresh look on the prime minister's face, belonging to a judge in Scott.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' signals the anagram of BLAIR MIEN. A birlieman is a Scots word, used by Sir Walter Scott, for a local referee settling neighbours' disputes.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots, used by Walter Scott, the word names a parish umpire chosen to settle disputes between neighbours.

clue.text: Sir Robert Stephenson… Boer War historian, and a jolly good scout

definitions.text: Sir Robert Stephenson… Boer War historian, and a jolly good scout

parts.words: Sir Robert Stephenson… Boer War historian, and a jolly good scout
parts.note: the founder of the Scout movement was Robert Stephenson ___ Baden-Powell, defender of Mafeking, who wrote on the Boer War; the missing middle name is wanted

explanation.surface: Fill in the name of the Boer War writer who founded the Scouts.
explanation.walkthrough: Baden-Powell's full name was Robert Stephenson Smyth Baden-Powell; the dots mark the gap the answer fills.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scout founder's third given name completes the sequence of his names printed in the clue.

clue.text: Wharton is possibly historical novelist

indicators.note: possibly says the letters could be arranged another way

explanation.surface: Suggests that Edith Wharton might count as a writer of historical fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' signals the anagram of WHARTON IS. William Harrison Ainsworth wrote historical romances such as The Tower of London.
explanation.definitionFit: William Harrison Ainsworth was a Victorian writer of historical romances such as Old St Paul's.

clue.text: "Too swift arrives as — as too slow" (Romeo and Juliet)

definitions.text: "Too swift arrives as — as too slow" (Romeo and Juliet)

parts.words: "Too swift arrives as — as too slow" (Romeo and Juliet)
parts.note: Friar Laurence's warning to Romeo about haste; the missing word means late

explanation.surface: A Shakespeare line with a word left out for the solver to supply.
explanation.walkthrough: Friar Laurence says 'Too swift arrives as tardy as too slow', meaning haste delays you as much as dawdling.
explanation.definitionFit: The gap in the line takes a word meaning late or behindhand, the opposite of swift.

clue.text: Frank but manipulative friend of the scion of Hermiston

definitions.text: Frank but manipulative friend of the scion of Hermiston

parts.words: Frank but manipulative friend of the scion of Hermiston
parts.note: in Stevenson's Weir of Hermiston, the judge's son Archie is befriended and betrayed by Frank, whose surname is wanted

explanation.surface: An open-seeming yet scheming companion of a young heir.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frank' looks like an adjective (candid) contrasting with 'manipulative', but it is the character's first name.
explanation.definitionFit: In Stevenson's unfinished Weir of Hermiston, Frank is the false friend of Archie Weir, heir to the estate.

clue.text: Artisan whose village was deserted

definitions.meaning: a craftsman working in precious metal
Oliver, the Irish writer, wrote the poem The Deserted Village

explanation.definitionFit: A craftsman who makes jewellery from precious metal, and also the surname of the poet of The Deserted Village.

clue.text: Point of departure is to let wine breathe, Hailey suggests?

definitions.meaning: a place where flights take off
to expose the fortified drink to the air, read as two words

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hailey suggests' points to Arthur Hailey's bestselling novel of that name; the second definition splits the answer into AIR PORT.
explanation.definitionFit: A place from which aircraft leave, and, split in two, airing a fortified wine before drinking.

clue.text: A. P. Herbert pointed out that there was none to fun in any Act of Parliament

definitions.text: A. P. Herbert pointed out that there was none to fun in any Act of Parliament

parts.words: A. P. Herbert pointed out that there was none to fun in any Act of Parliament
parts.note: Herbert, humorist and MP, quipped that no Act of Parliament ever mentions fun; the missing word is the one meaning a mention

explanation.surface: A humorous MP observes that statutes never mention enjoyment.
explanation.walkthrough: A. P. Herbert's line is 'There is no reference to fun in any Act of Parliament'; the word is supplied from the quotation.
explanation.definitionFit: A mention or allusion to something, which Herbert said statute law never makes to fun.

clue.text: Harm in a demonized demon

indicators.note: demonized suggests the letters are possessed and thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: Damage inflicted by a fiend made more fiendish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Demonized' signals the anagram of HARM IN A. Ahriman is the evil spirit of Zoroastrian belief.
explanation.definitionFit: In Zoroastrianism the evil spirit, opponent of Ahura Mazda, is called Angra Mainyu or Ahriman.

clue.text: Contribution by late order batsman recorded by creator of the coup?

definitions.meaning: a weak tail-end batsman in cricket is a rabbit, and what he adds to the score is a run

definitions.text: recorded by creator of the coup?
definitions.meaning: John Updike, author of The Coup, wrote the novel about Harry Angstrom

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a rabbit is a hopeless batsman low in the order. 'The Coup' is an Updike novel; his Rabbit, Run is the first Angstrom book.
explanation.definitionFit: A single scored by a hapless tail-ender, and the title of Updike's 1960 novel.

clue.text: Attested to an editor's error?

indicators.note: an error in the text means the letters are set out wrongly

parts.note: the letters of 'an editor's', including the s, are the fodder

explanation.surface: A document is certified as accurate with respect to a mistake by an editor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Error' signals the anagram of AN EDITORS; 'to' is a link. The editor's error looks like the subject, but it is the jumbling.
explanation.definitionFit: A document certified by a notary, a public official, has been formally witnessed and authenticated.

clue.text: Strindberg's account of Dis territory?

definitions.meaning: the Swedish dramatist's autobiographical book of his 1890s crisis bears the Italian word for hell
Dis is the Roman underworld god, and his realm is hell, as in Dante

explanation.walkthrough: The OCR dropped the D of 'Dis', Pluto's name and Dante's city of hell.
explanation.definitionFit: Strindberg's 1897 book takes Dante's word for hell, the domain of the underworld god.

clue.text: Porter's account of Mrs Antony?

definitions.meaning: Anna Maria Porter, the Regency novelist, wrote a novel with this woman's name as its title

explanation.walkthrough: 'Porter' looks like a doorman or the drink, but it is the novelist Anna Maria Porter.
explanation.definitionFit: Octavian's sister married Mark Antony, and the same name titles a novel by Anna Maria Porter.

clue.text: Ministers of Boothby who had something to hide

definitions.meaning: the senior ministers of a government

definitions.text: Boothby who had something to hide

explanation.walkthrough: Guy Boothby's 1900 novel is A Cabinet Secret, so his cabinet had something hidden.
explanation.definitionFit: The body of senior government ministers, and the first word of Boothby's novel title about a secret.

clue.text: Skilled worker explained the art of creation

definitions.meaning: a tradesman who works in wood
Edward, the Victorian social thinker, wrote The Art of Creation (1904)

explanation.walkthrough: Edward Carpenter, English socialist writer, published The Art of Creation in 1904.
explanation.definitionFit: A woodworking tradesman, and the surname of the author of The Art of Creation.

clue.text: Airborne heart consultant

parts.note: a flying figure who deals in matters of the heart, love rather than cardiology

explanation.surface: A cardiologist who works in the air, perhaps on a flying ambulance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heart consultant' suggests a cardiologist; it is the winged Roman god of love.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman god of love is a winged boy who shoots arrows into hearts.

clue.text: For example, bad actor suggests location for celebration of Magna Carta

definitions.text: location for celebration of Magna Carta

parts.note: EG is the abbreviation for exempli gratia, for example
a ham is an overacting performer

explanation.surface: Says a poor performer indicates the place where the Great Charter is commemorated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suggests' is a link. Egham is the Surrey town by Runnymede, where King John sealed Magna Carta in 1215.
explanation.definitionFit: The Surrey town lies beside Runnymede meadow, where the 1215 charter is commemorated by a memorial.

clue.text: Sort of play by Beatrice Harraden

definitions.text: Sort of play by Beatrice Harraden

parts.words: Sort of play by Beatrice Harraden
parts.note: Harraden's 1908 novel title is a compound ending in 'play'; the missing first part is wanted

explanation.surface: Asks what kind of drama a Victorian novelist wrote.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play' looks like a stage drama, but the title of Harraden's novel is Interplay; the answer is the part before 'play'.
explanation.definitionFit: Placed before 'play' it makes the title of Beatrice Harraden's novel.

clue.text: "From what old, ancestral, be it Eagle, Bear or Beaver…" (Longfellow, Hiawatha)

definitions.text: "From what old, ancestral, be it Eagle, Bear or Beaver…" (Longfellow, Hiawatha)

parts.words: "From what old, ancestral, be it Eagle, Bear or Beaver…" (Longfellow, Hiawatha)
parts.note: the line in Hiawatha asks after a family's emblem animal; the missing word is the clan emblem of the line

explanation.surface: A line from Longfellow's poem with its key word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The line in The Song of Hiawatha reads 'From what old, ancestral Totem, Be it Eagle, Bear, or Beaver'.
explanation.definitionFit: An animal or object adopted as a clan's ancestral emblem, such as eagle, bear or beaver.

clue.text: A blow from a well known old review

definitions.meaning: the British humorous weekly magazine that ran from 1841 to 2002

explanation.definitionFit: A strike with the fist, and the famous British satirical magazine that ran for over 150 years.

clue.text: Worships seat Verne abandoned

indicators.note: abandoned, as in wild and unrestrained, tells us the letters run riot

explanation.surface: Someone adores the chair the French novelist left behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abandoned' looks like Verne leaving his seat, but it signals the anagram of SEAT VERNE.
explanation.definitionFit: To revere someone deeply is to hold them in worshipful regard.

clue.text: Grahame tales made new in carts

indicators.note: in places the remade letters inside the carts

parts.note: drays are low heavy carts for carrying loads

indicators.note: new means the letters of made are given a fresh order

explanation.surface: Kenneth Grahame's stories freshly produced in wagons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Made new' looks like a description of the tales being reissued, but 'new' is the anagram signal and 'in' the container. Dream Days is Kenneth Grahame's sequel to The Golden Age.
explanation.definitionFit: Kenneth Grahame's 1898 collection of childhood stories is the sequel to The Golden Age.

clue.text: Wanderer. Savage one for example? But by inference, perfectly sane

definitions.meaning: someone who roams without a fixed home
not crazy at all, which by inference splits as 'no' and 'mad'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Savage one for example?' hints at a wandering tribesman; 'by inference' warns that the second sense is the answer split as NO MAD.
explanation.definitionFit: A person of a roving tribe with no settled home, and, split in two, a phrase for not crazy.
